extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and practitioners interested in comparative blasphemy laws, freedom of expression, and human rights
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative summary of national laws, penal code provisions, and notable cases concerning blasphemy, insult to religion, and related offences across many countries and jurisdictions. Includes statutory text citations, typical penalties, and notable prosecutions or legal outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poland — offence of offending religious feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Offending religious feelings (e.g., insulting religion, interrupting religious ceremonies) is punishable by a fine, restriction of liberty or loss of liberty for up to 2 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by pro-Church politicians/activists; criticized as vague and abused to limit free speech. Notable convictions: Dorota 'Doda' Rabczewska fined 5,000 złoty (2012); Jerzy Urban fined 120,000 złoty (2019). 2022 proposals sought tougher penalties (e.g., three-year jail terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Romania — prohibition on infringing fundamental rights and liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: "Cults, religious associations and religious groups ... must not infringe upon ... fundamental human rights and liberties", with the Constitution including freedom of conscience and freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romania has not had active blasphemy laws; attempts to criminalize blasphemy (2011) were withdrawn. Recent administrative fines/warnings have been applied to artworks deemed 'obscenity' or 'mockery' (e.g., Paul Baraka exhibition, 2023).

rubrics_metrics.name: Russia — Article 148 (public actions offending religious feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal to conduct 'public actions expressing explicit disrespect for society and committed for the purpose of offending the religious feelings of believers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 2 increases punishments when coupled with desecration of holy symbols or religious texts. Enacted following Pussy Riot incident (2012–2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seychelles — Section 128 'wounding religious feelings'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 128 criminalises 'wounding religious feelings' with a penalty of imprisonment for a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory offence with a one-year maximum imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Africa — common law offence of blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasphemy defined as 'unlawfully, intentionally and publicly acting contemptuously towards God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writings suggest blasphemy may be unconstitutional under the 1994 Bill of Rights (freedom of expression), and discriminatory since it historically applied to Christianity. Notable historical prosecutions exist; enforcement has been rare. The Equality Act 2000 forbids hate speech based on religion but is civil, not criminal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spain — Penal Code article 525 'vilification' of religious feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 525 considers 'vilification' of religious 'feelings', 'dogmas', 'beliefs' or 'rituals'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted by some as very close to a blasphemy law; used in prosecutions (e.g., Javier Krahe). Political pledges have been made to repeal medieval laws on offending religious sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweden — no explicit blasphemy prohibition; laws protect groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Swedish laws do not explicitly prohibit blasphemy; instead, legislation protects minority groups via acts against 'agitation against a specific group of people' covering race, origin, faith, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal provisions applied for 'agitation against a specific group' (e.g., Quran burnings led to prosecutions and suspended sentences). The legal framework focuses on protecting practitioners rather than religion itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Switzerland — Article 261 (Attack on the freedom of faith and worship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who publicly and maliciously insults or mocks religious convictions, desecrates objects or places intended for worship, or maliciously prevents/disrupts/publicly mocks an act of worship "shall be liable to a monetary penalty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory definition lists malicious public insults, desecrations, and disruptions; penalty is monetary rather than imprisonment per quoted text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tanzania (mainland) — sacrilege and wounding religious feelings (Articles 125 and 129)
rubrics_metrics.description: Penal Code criminalises acts of sacrilege (destroying/damaging/defiling sacred buildings or objects) and uttering words with intent to wound religious feelings; both are misdemeanours punishable by up to one year imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zanzibar has separate Penal Decree Act with similar offences and penalties up to two years and/or fine. Enforcement information not always available. Notable case: Eva Abdulla (acquitted on appeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuvalu — Section 127 'wounding religious feelings'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 127 of the Tuvalu Penal Code criminalises 'wounding religious feelings' with penalty of imprisonment for a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-year maximum imprisonment statutory provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Kingdom — historical blasphemy offences and abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: England and Wales abolished common law offences of blasphemy and blasphemous libel in 2008; Scotland decriminalised in 2021 with common law offence abolished from 1 April 2024; Northern Ireland retains common law offence but not recently used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical prosecutions cited (e.g., Whitehouse v. Lemon 1977). Legislative changes driven by Law Commission recommendations. Certain media/stage exceptions applied (Theatres Act 1968 and Broadcasting Act 1990).

rubrics_metrics.name: British Virgin Islands — Section 289 (public abusive/blasphemous language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminalises use of 'abusive, blasphemous, indecent, insulting, profane or threatening language' in a public place; punishable by up to three months imprisonment or a fine up to US$250.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory local offence with short custodial term or small fine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Montserrat — Section 325 (public abusive/blasphemous language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 325 criminalises use of 'abusive, blasphemous, indecent, insulting, profane or threatening language' in a public place; punishable by up to three months imprisonment or a fine up to US$250.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar small-penalty statutory offence as in some British territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States — historical blasphemy prosecutions and constitutional protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically had blasphemy as proscribed speech; modern constitutional doctrine (e.g., Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson, 1952) protects sacrilegious content under freedom of speech and press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some state/corporate-name statutes (e.g., Pennsylvania corporate name prohibition) were struck down as unconstitutional (Kalman case, 2010). Federal sentencing guidelines can increase penalties for bias-motivated crimes (Section 3A1.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Muslim-majority countries — Sharia influence and severe penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: In many Muslim-majority countries, values from Islam influence laws criminalising blasphemy, often attached to heavy punishments; Islamic sources (hadiths) suggest various punishments including death in some interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Quran admonishes blasphemy but does not specify punishment; hadiths supply potential penalties. Consequences and enforcement vary widely by country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afghanistan — blasphemy under Sharia (execution possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Islamic emirate, Afghanistan prohibits blasphemy as an offence under Sharia; blasphemy can be punished by retaliatory penalties up to and including execution by hanging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since Taliban takeover (2021), arrests for blasphemy have occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algeria — penal (retaliatory) legislation against blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Algeria's constitution declares Islam the state religion, Algeria uses retaliatory legislation rather than Sharia to combat blasphemy; penalty can be up to 5 years imprisonment and a fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory penalties rather than explicit Sharia death-penalty prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bangladesh — 'hurting religious sentiments' offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Bangladesh forbids blasphemy via provisions in its penal code prohibiting 'hurting religious sentiments' and other laws/policies restricting freedom of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political leaders have resisted calls for harsher penalties (e.g., death penalty) and emphasize existing laws to handle offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egypt — Article 98(f) (propagating extreme ideas to incite strife or ridicule religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 98(f): confinement 6 months to 5 years, or fine 500–1000 pounds, for using religion to propagate extreme ideas for the purpose of inciting strife, ridiculing or insulting a heavenly religion/sect, or damaging national unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory text with imprisonment/fine ranges; used to prosecute 'ridiculing' or 'insulting' religious topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indonesia — Article 156(a) (public expressions of hostility/contempt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 156(a) forbids deliberately, in public, expressing feelings of hostility, hatred, or contempt against religions with the purpose of preventing others from adhering to any religion, and forbids disgracing a religion; penalty up to five years imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in high-profile convictions (e.g., Basuki Tjahaja Purnama, Ahok).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iran — blasphemy law derived from Sharia
rubrics_metrics.description: Iran, an Islamic theocracy, derives laws against blasphemy from Sharia; laws complement other offences such as insulting Islam and publishing materials deviating from Islamic standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharia-based criminal framework; enforcement and penalties often severe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan — Articles 273 and 278 (scorning prophets; insulting religious feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 273 criminalizes 'scorning or reviling any of the Prophets' with imprisonment up to three years; Article 278 criminalizes 'publishing anything that would insult the religious feelings or religious beliefs of other people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions address both reviling prophets and publishing insulting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kuwait — cybercrime law Article 6 (insulting sacred figures/material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 6 of Kuwait's cybercrime laws mentions punishment up to 12 months in prison and a 20,000 KWD (approx US$66,000) fine for insulting 'God, the Holy Quran, Prophets, the Noble Companions of Prophet Muhammad, Wives of the Prophet, or persons who are part of the Prophet's family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cybercrime provisions with significant fines and imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malaysia — prevention by education, media restrictions and legal system
rubrics_metrics.description: Malaysia prevents insult to religion via education, broadcasting/publishing restrictions, Sharia courts in some states, and the Malaysian Penal Code where Sharia is not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hybrid system: state-level Sharia courts for Muslims and secular penal code provisions for others; uses administrative/media controls as well as criminal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mauritania — apostasy and 'Act of Indecency toward Islam' (Article 306)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime of apostasy is defined under 'Act of Indecency toward Islam'; Article 306 invites a Muslim guilty of apostasy to repent within three days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory apostasy process with religiously framed criminal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nigeria — section 204 and Sharia courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Nigeria prohibits blasphemy by section 204 of its Criminal Code and permits Sharia courts to operate in some states, which may also criminalize blasphemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vigilantism frequently usurps jurisdiction of courts; enforcement and severity vary by region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Northern Cyprus — blasphemy criminalised but rarely enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the U.S. Department of State, blasphemy is criminalised in Northern Cyprus, but the law is rarely enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De jure criminalisation with limited practical enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pakistan — detailed penal code sections (§295–§298-C) and death penalty under §295-C
rubrics_metrics.description: Pakistan's Penal Code Chapter XV includes §§295–298-C covering injuring/defiling places of worship, deliberate malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings, defiling the Holy Qur'an, derogatory remarks about the Prophet, disturbing religious assembly, etc.; §295-C carries the death penalty for blasphemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex statutory scheme; prosecutions typically target minorities (Ahmadiyya, Christians) but have increasingly affected other Muslims; accused, officials, lawyers, judges have faced harassment and violence. High political sensitivity (e.g., assassination of Shahbaz Bhatti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Palestine (Palestinian National Authority) — multiple civil/military provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: PNA has provisions in civil and military law used against alleged online blasphemy; cases have been prosecuted as incitement, insulting religious leaders, and offending religious views (e.g., Waleed Al-Husseini).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charges may rely on older Jordanian laws still in force in the West Bank; prosecutions have led to detention and international pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qatar — jail up to seven years and fines for defaming Islam
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalty for committing blasphemy in Qatar is a jail sentence of up to seven years; defamation of Islam by producing/promoting defamatory imagery carries one-year prison or QR1,000 fine. Religious criticism on websites is censored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State monitors imported broadcasts for sensitive religious content; blasphemy accusations may be used as evidence of apostasy (a separate offence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Saudi Arabia — Sharia-based penalties up to death
rubrics_metrics.description: Saudi Arabia's law is an amalgam of Sharia, royal edicts and fatawa, prescribing penalties up to the death penalty for blasphemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement under a strict religious legal framework; high-profile arrests (e.g., Raif Badawi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudan — Section 125 (insulting religion, inciting hatred; penalties include imprisonment, fine, lashes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 125 prohibits 'insulting religion, inciting hatred and showing contempt for religious beliefs' with penalties including imprisonment, a fine, and up to forty lashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in notable cases (e.g., Sudanese teddy bear case); reforms: Sudan repealed its apostasy law in July 2020 but blasphemy law suggested for repeal by USCIRF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turkey — Article 216 (provoking rancour; disrespecting religious beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 216 criminalizes openly provoking rancour or hostility between groups, openly humiliating a person because of group identity, and openly disrespecting the religious belief of a group (imprisonment ranges one year to three years, or six months to one year for humiliation/disrespect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to public statements and social media (e.g., Fazıl Say investigated and initially sentenced for Twitter posts; conviction later reversed on appeal citing freedom of thought/expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: United Arab Emirates — Article 312 (blasphemy and related public offences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 312 prescribes jail of at least one year or a fine for public offences including offence to Islamic sacred beliefs, insult to divine recognized religions, approving/encouraging sinful actions, and knowingly eating pork meat by Muslims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of public offences that can trigger imprisonment or fines; controls extend to behaviour considered offensive to religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yemen — Sharia-influenced prosecutions and vigilantism (unsourced in text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations of blasphemy in Yemen often target minorities, intellectuals, artists, reporters and human rights defenders; vigilante or official abuse can kill the accused or force exile; accused are subject to Islamic law with some interpretations prescribing death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section flagged as lacking sources in the text; describes pattern of severe consequences including killings and exile in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: China — state censorship and punishment for religious insults
rubrics_metrics.description: China (officially atheist) has banned publications and arrested authors for content alleged to insult Islam (e.g., book 'Xing Fengsu' banned, authors arrested in 1989); state media advocated limiting freedom of speech after Charlie Hebdo attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government has at times acquiesced to religious protests and used censorship; enforcement uneven across ethnic/religious groups (Hui vs Uyghurs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Israel — Articles 170 (insult to religion) and 173 (injury to religious sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 170: destroying/desecrating a sacred place/object with intent to revile religion — liable to three years' imprisonment. Article 173: publishing or voicing words/sounds in public likely to crudely offend religious faith — liable to one year imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rarely enforced, but notable conviction: right-wing activist sentenced to two years for leaflets picturing Muhammed as a pig (1997).

rubrics_metrics.name: India — Section 295A (deliberate and malicious intention to outrage religious feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 295A prevents 'insulting' religions with 'deliberate and malicious intention of outraging religious feelings' and has been used as a de facto blasphemy law; it was introduced in 1927 to prevent hate speech that insults religion and to maintain public order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key distinction from English common law: requirement of 'deliberate and malicious intention'. Section used multiple times; remains a threat to freedom of expression in practice.
